meta.case_name: Loyalty Card Scheme for Canadian Supermarket (McKinsey)

prompt.context: Our client is a major supermarket chain in Canada. They are one of three major players in this sector and the rest of the market is split amongst smaller, regional firms. In January 2000, they introduced a loyalty card scheme (run by a third party provider), but have not been able to make this scheme successful. The CEO has called us in to review their program and suggest ways to improve it.
prompt.question: What areas should we investigate to determine the performance of this scheme, and how can it be improved?

clarifying_info.q: How does the loyalty card work?
clarifying_info.a: For every $1 spent in store, the customer receives 1 point. These points can be redeemed for discounts at the store. 100 points can be redeemed for a 1% saving on every $100 spent.

clarifying_info.q: What is the total number of transactions?
clarifying_info.a: The total number of transactions is 10 million.

exhibits.title: Loyalty Card vs. Non-Loyalty Card Transactions
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the percentage of transactions and the percentage of total spend split between loyalty card holders and non-loyalty card holders.
exhibits.data: Non-loyalty card: approximately 67% of transactions, approximately 60% of total spend. Loyalty card: approximately 33% of transactions, approximately 40% of total spend. Total spend figure shown.

exhibits.title: Number of Supermarket Loyalty Cards in Wallet
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the distribution of how many supermarket loyalty cards customers carry in their wallet (0, 1, 2, or 3 cards).
exhibits.data: Two peaks in the distribution: one at 0 cards and one at 3 cards; bars at 1 and 2 cards are shorter.

framework: Define the goals of the scheme: profitability, business intelligence, or customer retention
Benchmark the potential profitability of loyalty card schemes against competitors or grocery stores in other regions
Compare actual profitability of this scheme — identify any gap and its root causes
Model value drivers: Total customers x % customers with card x extra profits per customer. Extra profits per customer depend on increased visit frequency and spend per visit
Assess the cost structure of the scheme (discounts, software, promotion, customer support, third-party provider fees)
Consider alternatives: other pricing, promotion, or customer loyalty schemes that could match or surpass the loyalty card scheme

questions.prompt: What are the costs associated with running a loyalty card program?
questions.guidance: Discounts (the largest cost), software upgrades to registers, promotion of the scheme, customer support, and third-party provider costs such as printing cards and maintaining data (likely paid on a per-customer rate to the third-party provider).

questions.prompt: (a) How would you interpret the transaction and spend data in Exhibit 1? (b) Calculate the average revenue per transaction for loyalty card holders and for non-loyalty-card customers.
questions.guidance: (a) A large share of transactions are from non-loyalty-card customers, suggesting many customers are unaware of or not enrolled in the scheme — there is growth potential. However this is per-transaction data, not per-customer, so we cannot directly infer the number of cardholders. Loyalty card transactions show higher spend per transaction, but this could reflect selection bias (frequent shoppers self-select into the card) rather than a causal card effect. (b) Use: Spend per transaction = (Total $ spend x % $ share) / (Total # transactions x % transaction share). Total spend = $300MM, total transactions = 10 million.

math.setup: Spend per transaction = (Total $ spend x % $ spend share) / (Total # transactions x % # transactions share). Loyalty card: ~40% of spend, ~1/3 of transactions. Non-loyalty: ~60% of spend, ~2/3 of transactions.
steps: Loyalty card: ($300MM x 40%) / (10M x 1/3) = $120MM / 3.33M = $36 per transaction
Non-loyalty card: ($300MM x 60%) / (10M x 2/3) = $180MM / 6.67M = $27 per transaction
math.answer: Loyalty card holders spend ~$36 per transaction vs. ~$27 per transaction for non-loyalty card customers.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2 shows a bimodal distribution of supermarket loyalty cards in customers' wallets. What does this tell you?
questions.guidance: Most customers either carry no loyalty cards or carry cards for three supermarkets (likely our client and the two other major chains). This means loyalty cards do not in practice drive loyalty to a single chain — customers carry and use whichever card matches the store they happen to visit. A segment has no card at all, suggesting unawareness or disinterest. Key implication: loyalty cards are unlikely to determine where someone shops, but they can influence what products and how much customers buy at a given store. The program should reflect this by offering bonus points on high-margin products.

recommendation: Run promotion campaigns to enroll more card members — a large share of transactions currently come from non-loyalty-card customers, representing significant growth potential
Give additional loyalty points for purchases of high-margin products to steer customers toward those items and improve scheme economics
Restructure the loyalty card formula to offer dollar-amount discounts on specific high-margin items rather than undifferentiated flat-rate rewards
risks: Loyalty cards may not drive true store loyalty if customers carry cards for all major competitors — increased enrollment may not translate to increased share of wallet
Promotion and discount costs could erode profitability if not carefully targeted to high-margin categories
Third-party provider rate structure may limit flexibility in redesigning the reward formula
next_steps: Quantify the incremental profit impact of targeting high-margin products with bonus points vs. the current flat-rate reward structure
Analyze competitor loyalty programs to benchmark reward generosity and identify differentiation opportunities
Model the enrollment growth scenario: estimate additional revenue from converting non-card transactions to card transactions and assess required promotion spend
